title: Trump Rolls Out New Tariffs on 60 Countries as India Faces 12.5% Levy
excerpt: The Section 301 tariffs, effective Friday, replace expiring emergency duties struck down by the Supreme Court, with rates of 10% to 12.5% covering 99% of U.S. imports.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Trump's administration imposes 12.5% tariffs on 60 countries, including India, effective Friday.
  • New tariffs replace a temporary 10% duty, following a Supreme Court ruling against previous tariffs.
  • Oil, gas, and certain products are exempt; tariffs won't stack with existing steel and aluminum duties.
  • India's exports to the U.S. reached $80 billion in fiscal year 2025, making it a key trading partner.
  • Average U.S. tariff levels could rise to 17% as new tariffs are implemented.
New Tariff Structure Unveiled

12.5%

New Tariff Regime Takes Shape

The Trump administration on Thursday unveiled sweeping new tariffs targeting 60 countries, effective at 12:01 a.m. Friday, in its most significant trade action since the Supreme Court dismantled the president's original tariff architecture earlier this year.

The duties, imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, are split into two tiers. Countries that have not enacted forced labor laws — including India, China, Japan and South Korea — will face a 12.5% tariff. Those with existing but insufficiently enforced labor protections, such as Canada, Mexico and the European Union, will pay 10%. The tariffs cover 99.4% of U.S. imports, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative.

"Today's action is the most sweeping international labor rights action the U.S. has ever taken — that any country has ever taken," a senior administration official told reporters.

Legal Reset After Supreme Court Ruling

The move reconstructs the administration's tariff regime on firmer legal ground. In February, the Supreme Court ruled that Trump's April 2025 "Liberation Day" tariffs — imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act — were unconstitutional. Trump responded with a temporary 10% tariff under Section 122, capped at 150 days and expiring Friday.

Section 301 tariffs require a formal investigation and comment period — the USTR received more than 1,500 submissions from businesses — but can remain in place indefinitely, making them more durable than emergency powers.

"The specific authorities this administration is using have changed, but the trade strategy has not."

— Jamieson Greer, U.S. Trade Representative

Critics have accused the White House of using the forced labor investigation as a legal vehicle to reimpose duties at similar levels. A senior administration official dismissed that framing as "simplistic."

Exemptions and No Stacking

The new Section 301 rates will not stack on existing tariffs. Steel and aluminum imports, already at 50% under Section 232, stay at that level. Oil and gas are fully exempt. The administration is also negotiating bilateral carve-outs for products critical to the U.S. economy but impossible to source domestically, including certain pharmaceutical ingredients.

For most Americans, the shift is unlikely to produce an immediate price shock since the new rates roughly mirror the expiring 10% duty. Federal Reserve economists have estimated existing tariffs raised core goods prices by about 3.4% through February, adding roughly 0.8 percentage points to overall core inflation.

India in the Higher Bracket

India is among more than 40 nations placed in the 12.5% tier — a rate that could pressure key export sectors including textiles, pharmaceuticals and IT hardware. The classification stems from the USTR's determination that India has not enacted forced labor prohibitions meeting U.S. standards.

Impact on India-U.S. Trade
›India faces pressure on key export sectors like textiles and pharmaceuticals.
›Merchandise exports from India to the U.S. totaled $80 billion in FY 2025.
›Negotiations for a bilateral trade framework are ongoing between India and the U.S.

The tariff arrives at a sensitive juncture for India-U.S. trade relations, with New Delhi and Washington negotiating a bilateral trade framework. India's merchandise exports to the U.S. totaled roughly $80 billion in fiscal year 2025, making it the country's largest trading partner.

Broader Trade War Intensifies

The Section 301 tariffs are one front in a widening trade campaign. On Wednesday, a separate 25% tariff hit Brazilian goods from farm machinery to ethanol. Earlier this week, Trump announced 50% tariffs on certain Canadian goods under a never-before-used provision of the 1930 Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act.

A separate Section 301 investigation into industrial overproduction by China and other nations could produce tariff proposals next month. Once all pending actions take effect, average U.S. tariff levels could reach about 17%, up from roughly 11% under the temporary regime, according to Drew DeLong, a former State Department official now at consulting firm Kearney.

"There's a great deal of support among businesses for the Administration's goal to encourage more production in the United States, but frequently changing the rules and ramping up new tariffs every few weeks isn't the way to do it."

— Jake Colvin, President, National Foreign Trade Council
Widening Trade War Landscape
›Separate 25% tariffs imposed on Brazilian goods.
›50% tariffs announced on certain Canadian goods.
›Average U.S. tariff levels projected to rise to 17%.

What's Next

The USTR must issue a final report in the forced labor investigation before the tariffs can be locked in permanently. The administration is also renegotiating the USMCA, with a third round of Mexico talks underway this week. Talks with Canada have not formally opened, and the 50% tariff has added fresh tension.

Brazil has rejected the 12.5% tariff on its goods. Mexico's economy minister said the effective tariff rate Mexico pays would not change. How India and other nations in the higher tier respond will shape the next phase of a trade war that shows no sign of easing.
